title: Step Away From the Speaker
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer opens his Most Common Actions (MCA) series with a small but generalisable observation from lesson-observation feedback: when a teacher asks a student a question and then physically steps toward them to hear the answer, it inadvertently signals to the rest of the class that they're excused from listening. Using a short classroom vignette (Mr B and Danny), Boxer shows how proximity and sustained eye contact with one student narrow what should be a whole-class interaction into a two-person conversation, undermining both audibility for the rest of the room and a culture of shared participation. His proposed fix is counterintuitive but simple: step away from the speaking student, break eye contact with them, and scan the rest of the room instead, which both makes the student project their voice more and keeps everyone else visibly accountable for listening. Boxer frames the piece as the template for an ongoing series built from patterns he notices repeatedly while observing a lot of lessons and giving feedback - small, specific, generalisable action steps rather than sweeping pedagogical theory. He introduces his WHENWHYBY structure (the context in which an action applies, the underlying purpose, and the concrete action itself) as the format that will structure every future MCA post, crediting Teach Like a Champion and Get Better Faster as his main influences.
points: Boxer diagnoses a subtle default behavior - stepping toward the student who answers - as inadvertently signalling to the rest of the class that they can switch off, since physical proximity and eye contact narrow the interaction to just two people.

His fix reverses the default: step away from the speaker, break eye contact with them, and face the room instead, so both audibility and whole-class attention improve through body positioning alone, without saying anything.

Boxer frames this as the first entry in his Most Common Actions (MCA) series, a deliberately narrow format - one small, generalisable action step per post - built from patterns he sees repeatedly while giving lesson observation feedback.

His WHENWHYBY structure (When this applies, Why it matters, By what specific action) is designed to make coaching feedback both context-bound and genuinely actionable, rather than a vague generic tip.
quotes: Mr B asks Danny a question. Danny’s answer is quiet, so Mr B steps towards him and says “could you speak up?” Danny repeats his answer and Mr B says “thank you” and continues with his teaching sequence.

This is obviously not good, as in the short term it means the other students are missing out on what could be a valuable answer from Danny or valuable feedback from Mr B, and over the long term means that a culture of low participation ratio can develop.
By stepping towards one student, keeping eye contact with them and addressing them directly, you subconsciously communicate to the rest of the room that they don’t need to be listening now.
By moving across the room, breaking eye contact and keeping his body facing as much of the room as possible, he communicates to every member of the class that they cannot switch off at this point.
By scanning the room rather than focusing on Danny, he can see if students appear to be listening or not.
The posts are going to be very short, and will focus on small things teachers can do to make their classrooms more inclusive and hopefully lead to high participation and levels of thought.
